Appendix A Proof

A.1 Proof of Theorem 1

See 1

Proof.

Algorithm 1 implements a rejection sampling scheme where sample xx is accepted with probability Paccept​(x)P_{\text{accept}}(x). The proof proceeds by showing that the acceptance probability Paccept​(x)=P​(x)1/TP_{\text{accept}}(x)=P(x)^{1/T}, so the rejection sampling procedure yields the desired normalized sample distribution:

PT​(x)=Paccept​(x)∑xPaccept​(x)=P​(x)1/T∑xP​(x)1/T.P_{T}(x)=\frac{P_{\text{accept}}(x)}{\sum_{x}P_{\text{accept}}(x)}=\frac{P(x)^{1/T}}{\sum_{x}P(x)^{1/T}}. (16)

The inverse temperature is decomposed as 1/T=n+α1/T=n+\alpha, where n=⌊1/T⌋n=\lfloor 1/T\rfloor is the integer part and α∈[0,1)\alpha\in[0,1) is the fractional part. The acceptance probability is the product of the success probabilities of the two corresponding stages.

Stage 1 (Integer Part): For the algorithm to proceed to stage 2 with a candidate sample xx, it must first draw xx for nn consecutive times in stage 1. As each draw is independent with probability P⁡(x)P(x), the probability of passing stage 1 with candidate xx is P​(x)nP(x)^{n}.

Stage 2 (Fractional Part): Let p=P⁡(x)p=P(x). The probability of acceptance in stage 2 is the cumulative probability of being accepted at any given iteration i≥1i\geq 1:

Pstage2\displaystyle P_{\text{stage2}} =P⁡(accept at ​i=1)+P⁡(pass ​i=1,accept at ​i=2)+…\displaystyle=P(\text{accept at }i=1)+P(\text{pass }i=1,\text{accept at }i=2)+\dots (17)
=p+(1−p)​(1−α1)​p+(1−p)2​(1−α1)​(1−α2)​p+…\displaystyle=p+(1-p)\left(1-\frac{\alpha}{1}\right)p+(1-p)^{2}\left(1-\frac{\alpha}{1}\right)\left(1-\frac{\alpha}{2}\right)p+\dots
=p​∑k=0∞(1−p)k​∏j=1k(1−αj)\displaystyle=p\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(1-p)^{k}\prod_{j=1}^{k}\left(1-\frac{\alpha}{j}\right)
=p​∑k=0∞(p−1)k​(α−1k)\displaystyle=p\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(p-1)^{k}\binom{\alpha-1}{k}
=p⋅(p−1+1)α−1\displaystyle=p\cdot(p-1+1)^{\alpha-1}
=pα.\displaystyle=p^{\alpha}.

The second to last step is due to the generalized binomial theorem.

Total Probability: The total probability of accepting a sample xx in a single trial is the product of the probabilities from the two stages:

Paccept​(x)=P​(x)n⋅P​(x)α=P​(x)1/T,P_{\text{accept}}(x)=P(x)^{n}\cdot P(x)^{\alpha}=P(x)^{1/T}, (18)

which completes the proof. ∎

A.2 Proof of Theorem 2

See 2

Proof.

The algorithm conducts series of independent trials, each with identical probability of success, and continues until one trial is successful, thereby following a geometric distribution. Therefore, the expected number of samples is the ratio of the expected number of samples per trial, 𝔼⁡[Nt​r​i​a​l]\mathbb{E}[N_{trial}], to the probability of a trial’s success, P⁡(success)P(\text{success}):

𝔼⁡[Nt​o​t​a​l]=𝔼⁡[Nt​r​i​a​l]P⁡(success).\mathbb{E}[N_{total}]=\frac{\mathbb{E}[N_{trial}]}{P(\text{success})}. (19)

Denominator (Success Probability): A trial is successful if any sample xx is accepted. The total success probability is the sum of acceptance probabilities over all possible outcomes:

P⁡(success)=∑xPaccept​(x)=∑xP​(x)1/T=ZT.P(\text{success})=\sum_{x}P_{\text{accept}}(x)=\sum_{x}P(x)^{1/T}=Z_{T}. (20)

Numerator (Expected Calls per Trial): Let Nt​r​i​a​lN_{trial} be the number of sampler calls in a single trial. A trial always involves N1N_{1} calls for stage 1 and may involve N2N_{2} calls for stage 2. The number of calls in Stage 1 is fixed at N1=nN_{1}=n. Thus, 𝔼⁡[N1]=n\mathbb{E}[N_{1}]=n.

If α=0\alpha=0, stage 2 is never performed, so 𝔼⁡[N2]=0\mathbb{E}[N_{2}]=0. If α>0\alpha>0, stage 2 is only executed if stage 1 succeeds with some candidate xx. Let ℰx\mathcal{E}_{x} be this event, so P⁡(ℰx)=P​(x)nP(\mathcal{E}_{x})=P(x)^{n}, and we have:

𝔼⁡[N2]=∑xP⁡(ℰx)⋅𝔼⁡[N2|ℰx].\mathbb{E}[N_{2}]=\sum_{x}P(\mathcal{E}_{x})\cdot\mathbb{E}[N_{2}|\mathcal{E}_{x}]. (21)

The conditional expectation 𝔼⁡[N2|ℰx]\mathbb{E}[N_{2}|\mathcal{E}_{x}] is the expected number of draws in stage 2 given candidate xx. Using the formula 𝔼⁡[X]=∑k=1∞P⁡(X≥k)\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}P(X\geq k), where XX is the number of draws in stage 2:

𝔼⁡[N2|ℰx]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[N_{2}|\mathcal{E}_{x}] =∑k=1∞P⁡(stage 2 requires at least ​k​ draws)\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}P(\text{stage 2 requires at least }k\text{ draws}) (22)
=∑k=0∞(1−P⁡(x))k​∏j=1k(1−αj).\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(1-P(x))^{k}\prod_{j=1}^{k}\left(1-\frac{\alpha}{j}\right).

This is the same sum we evaluated in Equation 17, which equals P​(x)α−1P(x)^{\alpha-1}. Therefore, if α>0\alpha>0:

𝔼⁡[N2]=∑xP​(x)n⋅P​(x)α−1=∑xP​(x)n+α−1=∑xP​(x)1/T−1.\mathbb{E}[N_{2}]=\sum_{x}P(x)^{n}\cdot P(x)^{\alpha-1}=\sum_{x}P(x)^{n+\alpha-1}=\sum_{x}P(x)^{1/T-1}. (23)

Combining the two cases, the total expected number of calls per trial is:

𝔼⁡[Ntrial]=𝔼⁡[N1]+𝔼⁡[N2]=n+𝕀⁡(α>0)​∑xP​(x)1/T−1.\mathbb{E}[N_{\text{trial}}]=\mathbb{E}[N_{1}]+\mathbb{E}[N_{2}]=n+\mathbb{I}(\alpha>0)\sum_{x}P(x)^{1/T-1}. (24)

Combining the numerator and denominator gives the final result:

𝔼⁡[Ntotal]=n+𝕀⁡(α>0)​∑xP​(x)1/T−1ZT.\mathbb{E}[N_{\text{total}}]=\frac{n+\mathbb{I}(\alpha>0)\sum_{x}P(x)^{1/T-1}}{Z_{T}}. (25)

∎

See 2.1

Proof.

The proof is divided into two cases based on the temperature range. We start from the general formula for the expected cost from Theorem 2:

𝔼⁡[Ntotal]=n+𝕀⁡(α>0)​∑xP​(x)1/T−1ZT.\mathbb{E}[N_{\text{total}}]=\frac{n+\mathbb{I}(\alpha>0)\sum_{x}P(x)^{1/T-1}}{Z_{T}}. (26)

Case 1: Low-Temperature Regime (0<T≤0.50<T\leq 0.5)

In this range, the exponent 1/T−1≥11/T-1\geq 1. Since P⁡(x)∈[0,1]P(x)\in[0,1], for any exponent β≥1\beta\geq 1, we have P​(x)β≤P⁡(x)P(x)^{\beta}\leq P(x). Thus, by summing over the entire sample space 𝒳\mathcal{X}:

∑x∈𝒳P​(x)1/T−1≤∑x∈𝒳P⁡(x)=1.\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}P(x)^{1/T-1}\leq\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}P(x)=1. (27)

The numerator of the cost formula is therefore bounded by n+1n+1:

n+𝕀⁡(α>0)​∑x∈𝒳P​(x)1/T−1≤n+𝕀⁡(α>0)⋅1≤n+1.n+\mathbb{I}(\alpha>0)\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}P(x)^{1/T-1}\leq n+\mathbb{I}(\alpha>0)\cdot 1\leq n+1. (28)

This establishes the bound for the low-temperature regime.

Case 2: High-Temperature Regime (0.5<T<10.5<T<1)

In this range,the exponent β=1/T−1\beta=1/T-1 is in the interval (0,1)(0,1). For such an exponent, the function f⁡(p)=pβf(p)=p^{\beta} is concave. By Jensen’s inequality, the sum ∑x∈𝒳P​(x)β\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}P(x)^{\beta} is maximized when P⁡(x)P(x) is a uniform distribution over the sample space, i.e., P⁡(x)=1/KP(x)=1/K for all x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}. The bound is:

∑x∈𝒳P​(x)1/T−1≤∑x∈𝒳(1K)1/T−1=K⋅(1K)1/T−1=K2−1/T.\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}P(x)^{1/T-1}\leq\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\left(\frac{1}{K}\right)^{1/T-1}=K\cdot\left(\frac{1}{K}\right)^{1/T-1}=K^{2-1/T}. (29)

Substituting this into the cost formula gives the bound for the high-temperature regime. This completes the proof. ∎

A.3 Proof of Theorem 3

See 3

Proof.

Let ℬ={x1,…,xN}\mathcal{B}=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{N}\} be a batch of NN samples drawn i.i.d. from the base distribution P⁡(x)P(x). For any sample x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, let CxC_{x} be the random variable for the count of xx in ℬ\mathcal{B}. The weight assigned to xx is Wx=(Cxn)W_{x}=\binom{C_{x}}{n}. Let XNX_{N} be the random variable for the probability of sampling xx from ℬ\mathcal{B}:

XN​(x)=Wx∑z∈𝒳Wz=(Cxn)∑z∈𝒳(Czn).X_{N}(x)=\frac{W_{x}}{\sum_{z\in\mathcal{X}}W_{z}}=\frac{\binom{C_{x}}{n}}{\sum_{z\in\mathcal{X}}\binom{C_{z}}{n}}. (30)

The overall probability we seek to analyze is the expectation of this random variable: Palg​(x,N)=𝔼⁡[XN]P_{\text{alg}}(x;N)=\mathbb{E}[X_{N}]. Our goal is to show that limN→∞𝔼⁡[XN]=PT​(x)\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[X_{N}]=P_{T}(x). The proof proceeds in two main steps: first, we show that the random variable XNX_{N} converges in probability to PT​(x)P_{T}(x); second, we use the Bounded Convergence Theorem to show that this implies the convergence of its expectation.

1. Convergence in Probability. By the Weak Law of Large Numbers, the proportion of occurrences of any sample xx converges in probability to its true probability P⁡(x)P(x):

CxN→𝑝P⁡(x)as ​N→∞.\frac{C_{x}}{N}\xrightarrow{p}P(x)\quad\text{as }N\to\infty. (31)

The weight WxW_{x} can be written as a polynomial in CxC_{x}, Wx=1n!​Cx​(Cx−1)​…​(Cx−n+1)W_{x}=\frac{1}{n!}C_{x}(C_{x}-1)\dots(C_{x}-n+1). We normalize this by NnN^{n}:

WxNn=1n!​(CxN)​(Cx−1N)​…​(Cx−n+1N).\frac{W_{x}}{N^{n}}=\frac{1}{n!}\left(\frac{C_{x}}{N}\right)\left(\frac{C_{x}-1}{N}\right)\dots\left(\frac{C_{x}-n+1}{N}\right). (32)

Since CxN→𝑝P⁡(x)\frac{C_{x}}{N}\xrightarrow{p}P(x) and kN→0\frac{k}{N}\to 0 for any constant kk, each term in the product converges to P⁡(x)P(x). By the Continuous Mapping Theorem, the entire expression converges in probability:

WxNn→𝑝1n!​P​(x)n.\frac{W_{x}}{N^{n}}\xrightarrow{p}\frac{1}{n!}P(x)^{n}. (33)

Now, we analyze the random variable XNX_{N} by dividing its numerator and denominator by NnN^{n}:

XN=Wx/Nn∑z∈𝒳(Wz/Nn).X_{N}=\frac{W_{x}/N^{n}}{\sum_{z\in\mathcal{X}}(W_{z}/N^{n})}. (34)

Applying the Continuous Mapping Theorem again for the ratio, we show that the random variable XNX_{N} converges in probability to PT​(x)P_{T}(x):

XN→𝑝1n!​P​(x)n∑z∈𝒳1n!​P​(z)n=P​(x)n∑z∈𝒳P​(z)n=PT​(x).X_{N}\xrightarrow{p}\frac{\frac{1}{n!}P(x)^{n}}{\sum_{z\in\mathcal{X}}\frac{1}{n!}P(z)^{n}}=\frac{P(x)^{n}}{\sum_{z\in\mathcal{X}}P(z)^{n}}=P_{T}(x). (35)

2. Convergence of Expectation. We have established that the random variable XNX_{N} converges in probability to PT​(x)P_{T}(x). Besides, we have that XNX_{N} is inherently bounded:

0≤XN=Wx∑z∈𝒳Wz≤1.0\leq X_{N}=\frac{W_{x}}{\sum_{z\in\mathcal{X}}W_{z}}\leq 1. (36)

We can now invoke the Bounded Convergence Theorem, which states that if a sequence of random variables XNX_{N} converges in probability to XX, and |XN|≤M|X_{N}|\leq M for all NN for some constant MM, then limN→∞𝔼⁡[XN]=𝔼⁡[limN→∞XN]\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[X_{N}]=\mathbb{E}[\lim_{N\to\infty}X_{N}]. Applying this theorem to our case:

limN→∞Palg​(x,N)=limN→∞𝔼⁡[XN]=𝔼⁡[limN→∞XN]=PT​(x).\lim_{N\to\infty}P_{\text{alg}}(x;N)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[X_{N}]=\mathbb{E}\left[\lim_{N\to\infty}X_{N}\right]=P_{T}(x). (37)

This completes the proof that the algorithm is asymptotically unbiased.
